- Karl Flinders, Chief reporter and senior editor EMEA

Capita’s outgoing boss championed the company’s tech transformation in a goodbye message to thousands of staff, but his years of work will be remembered for a tech project that went horribly wrong.

Adolfo Hernandez, who stepped down this week under mounting pressure , was tasked with transforming Capita’s delivery model through technology such as artificial intelligence (AI), but he leaves in the wake of a £239m Civil Service Pension Scheme (CSPS) project disaster , with an AI failure at its core, that has put the company’s future in doubt.

In a message to staff, Hernandez talked of Capita’s three-year journey under his leadership towards becoming a “technology-led, AI-enabled business services company”.

“Together, we reset the strategy, built an AI-led operating model with partners including Microsoft, AWS, Salesforce, Databricks, ServiceNow and Snowflake, rebuilt the leadership team, and saw our clients respond, with customer satisfaction at its highest since we began measuring it,” he wrote.

Hernandez outlined successes to thousands of Capita staff in his message: “That was not a small ambition for an organisation of our size and history, and you made it real: in how we work with our clients, in the platforms we’ve built, and in the way you’ve embraced new tools and new ways of working. This team improved renewal and win rates significantly.”

But he will be remembered as the CEO who was in charge when hundreds of civil servants were thrown into financial hardship because the company he led made a botch of their pensions.

## Tech disaster

But Hernandez did not ignore this in his goodbye, admitting it had “not got everything right”.

“I know the Civil Service Pension Scheme has asked a great deal of many of you, and I’m grateful to everyone working to restore the service members deserve,” he said.

The contract to administer the pensions of 1.7 million people was supposed to be a flagship project, demonstrating how AI technology could transform pension administration.

Capita was awarded the contract to run the administration of the CSPS in 2023, when the Cabinet Office handed it a seven-year contract worth £239m.

The contract was set to transfer from MyCSP to Capita in December 2025, allowing two years to prepare. However, as reported by Computer Weekly in October 2025, the Public Accounts Committee (PAC) warned there was a “real risk” that Capita would not be ready to take over in December . The supplier’s response to that claim was that it was inaccurate and “not reflective of the current state of the transition”.

But that did turn out to be the case, and within weeks of going live, the Cabinet Office appointed a troubleshooter to attempt to avert disaster. But it was too little too late, and disaster did strike.

During a joint PAC and Public Administration and Constitutional Affairs Committee (PACAC) hearing , PACAC chair Simon Hoare MP reminded Hernandez that the Cabinet Office was told: “The two-year transition period would lead to the digital artificial intelligence revolution to deliver a world-class, world-leading pension service.”

Hoare added: “None of that was met, neither the novel nor the basic.”

Hernandez conceded: “We have not been able to deploy the technology that would allow us to get there.”

## Financial trouble

Capita’s recent profit warning, with losses as a result of the failed Civil Service Pension Scheme expected to top £90m, its plunging share price and the need to raise £190m in the first half of next year are signs of a tough year ahead.

Add to this the UK government’s policy to insource more public sector work and the reluctance of ministers to sign off contracts with a firm that is making headlines for all the wrong reasons.

In May, Computer Weekly revealed ministers refused to sign off a £563m contract to Capita because of the CSPS problems. According to sources, Capita was set to be awarded the Learning Frameworks 2.0 contract, which provides access to learning, development and coaching for public sector organisations. It was planned as the replacement for existing learning and development contracts held by KPMG, but the government cancelled the procurement and will bring the service in-house.

MPs of all colours are rounding on Capita over the Synergy Business Process Services contract , which it won in March despite the CSPS problems. They are demanding Capita lose the deal, which, according to the official tender, has an estimated value of around £959m over 10 years. It supports back-office services for the Department for Work and Pensions, the Ministry of Justice, the Home Office, and the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs.

Capita has already been stripped of a contract to administer the Royal Mail pension scheme, which is being brought in-house after the supplier missed targets.

More pressure will inevitably come as prime minister Andy Burnham’s government policy to “move forward the biggest wave of insourcing in a generation” gathers momentum. Capita is almost solely reliant on UK public sector business.

The government has already said it is “actively shaping a long-term strategy to bring [the Civil Service] Pension Scheme back in-house”.

MPs of every party now have a line on Capita. Reform UK MP Richard Tice is the latest, who recently brought forward the urgent question in Parliament. He described his concern over a repeat of the collapse of Carillion following news that Hernandez was stepping down at Capita, alongside the profit warning and share price collapse.

Tice said the government should have a “plan B, a plan C and a plan D”, which “might involve ensuring that Capita can merge with another outsourcing company or underwriting the share issue, or it might have to involve taking it in-house”.
